title: The man washing the statue
translation: Someone was walking along the Koga road when he saw a man in nothing but the under-layers of court dress. He had pushed a wooden statue of a Buddhist saint down into the water of a rice field and was washing it very carefully. While the traveller stood there trying to make sense of it, two or three of his men appeared. "There you are, sir," they said, and they took him away.
It was the minister Koga. When he was himself, he was a perfectly proper, distinguished man.
original: ある{人|ひと}、{久我畷|こがなはて}を{通|とほ}りけるに、{小袖|こそで}に{大口|おほくち}きたる{人|ひと}、{木造|きづくり}の{地蔵|ぢざう}を{田|た}の{中|なか}の{水|みづ}におしひたして、ねんごろに{洗|あら}ひけり。
{心得|こころえ}がたく{見|み}るほどに、{狩衣|かりぎぬ}の{男|をとこ}{二人|ふたり}{三人|みたり}{出|い}で{来|き}て、「ここにおはしましけり。」とて、この{人|ひと}を{具|ぐ}して{往|い}にけり。
{久我|こが}{内大臣|ないだいじん}{殿|どの}にてぞおはしける。
{尋常|よのつね}におはしましける{時|とき}は、{神妙|しんべう}にやんごとなき{人|ひと}にておはしけり。
literal: When a certain person was passing along the Koga causeway, a person wearing a kosode and ōkuchi trousers had pushed a wooden Jizō down into the water in a rice field and was washing it carefully.
While he watched, unable to understand it, two or three men in hunting robes came out, said, 'So here you were', and went off taking this person with them.
It was the Koga Inner Minister.
When he was in his normal state, he was an admirably distinguished person.

notes.text: {畷|なはて}: a straight raised path between rice fields. The 1925 edition places this one south of Kyoto, west of Toba, running from the west bank of the Katsura river to Yamazaki. Koga, the family's estate, lay along it.
{小袖|こそで}: the undergarment, as the 1925 edition explains. {大口|おほくち}: wide-legged trousers worn under the outer trousers of formal court dress. So the man is in his underclothes, out in the fields.
The statue is of Jizō, a bodhisattva who looks after children, travellers and souls in hell. His statues, a shaved monk with a staff, still stand by roadsides all over Japan.
{狩衣|かりぎぬ}: originally hunting clothes, by this time the everyday wear of nobles and their men. These are his attendants.

notes.quote: ここにおはしましけり
notes.text: おはします: the highest respect language. Even while fetching their master out of a rice field, his men speak to him as they always do. けり here: discovery, 'so here you are'.

{内大臣|ないだいじん}: 'Inner Minister', one of the top posts at court. The 1925 edition identifies him as Koga Michimoto, son of Michitada, of a branch of the Minamoto. Modern commentaries agree: Michimoto (1240–1308) became Inner Minister in 1288. The next section tells a story about the same man.

notes.quote: 尋常におはしましける時は
notes.text: {尋常|よのつね}: 'normal, ordinary'. The 1925 edition points out that this hints at attacks of mental illness. Kenkō does not say so outright.
{神妙|しんべう}: here 'admirable, excellent'. Modern {神妙|しんみょう} has shifted to 'meek, well-behaved'.
